newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - German coalition, SPD agree to more tax talks.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - German coalition, SPD agree to more tax talks.

text.p: Germany's ruling parties and the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) agreed at talks on Monday to meet again this week to seek a compromise on tax-cutting reforms to fight record post-war unemployment.

Finance Minister Theo Waigel said a six-strong working group would meet again on Friday. Wolfgang Gerhardt, leader of junior coalition partners the Free Democrats (FDP) said he hoped a broad deal on tax reforms could be reached by Easter.

But the two sides ended a rare "summit" unhappy with each other's ideas of how to pay for tax cuts without throwing into doubt lasting compliance with the fiscal demands of European economic and monetary union (EMU).
"There was no narrowing of the gap between our two positions," SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine told a news conference after the three-hour talks.
Jolted by a January surge in unemployment to 4.7 million -- the highest since 1933 -- the two sides agreed to meet to try and agree reforms quickly.

Failure in the talks could condemn Waigel's two-year package of 30 billion marks ($17.9 billion) in tax cuts to a tough passage through parliament, where the SPD controls the upper house, and turn tax into a divisive issue at next year's general election.

Waigel has also said that the SPD must let through savings measures currently backed up in parliament if Germany is to meet the Maastricht treaty's budget deficit ceiling of three percent of GDP this year to qualify for EMU.

Although there appeared to have been no narrowing of basic differences at the initial tax summit, which Chancellor Helmut Kohl attended, Friday's talks will focus on cutting corporate taxes -- an issue where the sides are not far apart.
Waigel said the coalition side would be represented at the talks by the parliamentary leader of the Christian Democrats (CDU) Wolfgang Schaeuble, Hermann Otto Solms of the FDP and himself.
The SPD will send parliamentary faction leader Rudolf Scharping, North Rhine-Westphalia finance minister Heinz Schleusser and Hamburg mayor Henning Voscherau.

Coalition parties went into the talks determined to defend plans to cut personal income tax, with the bottom rate falling to 15 percent from 26 percent and the top rate slipping to 39 percent from 53 percent.

But Schleusser, the SPD's key numbers man, said Waigel's sums did not add up and pinpointed an extra 30 billion marks in revenue shortfalls which would have to be covered either by more borrowing or spending cutbacks.

The coalition is banking on an increase in value-added tax and faster economic growth to make up a financing gap of 44 billion marks. But the SPD opposes a VAT hike, a cut in top income tax and ending tax relief for unsocial work hours.
Schleusser said before the talks began that "the actual financing gap is clearly higher than 44 billion marks and cannot be justified."
Waigel, on his way into the talks, said Schleusser's figures were mistaken.
